source.title: Grokking on the Weight-Decay Clock: A Rate Hierarchy from Softly Broken Symmetries

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures delayed generalization on modular addition, but uses its own heavy-ball, coupled-weight-decay setup rather than reproducing the original training recipe. It also tests a distinct weight-decay-clock account in synthetic and nonlinear settings.
record.gate_note: The modular-addition benchmark reports training and test accuracy, and a sweep of time to a test-accuracy threshold. Synthetic experiments report population-risk and parameter-component relaxation, interventions, and optimizer comparisons. The paper does not vary training-set size. Mentions of circuits and adaptive optimizers in related work or limitations are not results testing those claims.
record.test_reason: The study's own modular-addition run (p = 17, width-128 quadratic MLP, full-batch heavy ball with coupled L2, large-norm init) shows test accuracy rising long after training accuracy saturates. That bears directly on V1. The setup differs from the original recipe, so this is T2. The synthetic linear-model results test the paper's own weight-decay-clock theory, not a listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors claim an exactly solvable post-interpolation weight-decay relaxation mechanism, carried by the population-active empirical-null subspace, that can contribute to grokking. They verify it without fitted parameters in a synthetic linear model, and reproduce the (1−β)/(ηλ) iteration law (slope 1.01) in a single-seed modular-addition benchmark. The accuracy-jump (margin) link, dataset-size laws, stochastic and adaptive optimizers, and multi-seed validation are left open.
record.recipe_differences: The study combines an exactly solvable linear heavy-ball analysis with a nonlinear modular-addition benchmark using p = 17, 158 training pairs, a width-128 quadratic MLP, full-batch heavy ball, and coupled L2. It reports a single-seed, single-architecture nonlinear result rather than an explicit replication of the original sources. The synthetic model uses Gaussian features and measures risk/component relaxation rather than algorithmic-task test accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: The relaxation rate and delay vary with η, λ, and β; the paper reports distinct clocks for coupled L2 versus decoupled weight decay. In the modular benchmark, frozen-projector component decay is slower than predicted, which the authors associate with Jacobian rotation during feature learning.

fits_no_version.finding: In the modular-addition sweep (27 configurations, same split and init), the iteration at which test accuracy reaches 0.9 scales with (1−β)/(ηλ), fitted log–log slope 1.01, over runs that reached threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The grokking delay scales inversely with ηλ/(1−β) under heavy ball with coupled L2.

fits_no_version.finding: In the solvable linear model, the population-active null component relaxes at the exact slow root ρ0 while training loss has no slow part. Rescaling that component shifts relaxation time logarithmically. Decoupled decay slows the clock by the factor (1−β).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-interpolation population-risk relaxation runs on an optimizer-dependent weight-decay clock carried by population-active empirical-null directions.

fits_no_version.finding: In modular addition, the test-loss tail decays at 4.5e-4 per step against a predicted 6.0e-4. The frozen-projector null component decays several times more slowly, which the authors attribute to Jacobian rotation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The frozen-projector local theory degrades quantitatively under feature learning in nonlinear grokking.

record.problems: The nonlinear benchmark is single-seed and single-architecture. No training-set-size sweep is reported. The study states that the frozen-projector description degrades quantitatively during modular-addition feature learning. The synthetic experiments are deterministic theorem/implementation checks rather than statistical evidence. The paper does not establish a margin-based link from population-loss relaxation to the abrupt test-accuracy jump.
record.rows_left_out: No additional reported results bearing on the claim versions were left out.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks; only one split (0.55) is used.
All parts: no circuit identification and no progress measures anticipating the accuracy jump.
All parts: no non-algorithmic data. Large-norm initialization is used but not varied as an on/off switch.
Efficient-circuit selection, critical dataset size and ungrokking; weight decay is studied only as a relaxation clock.
All parts; adaptive optimizers and numerical precision are not tested.

missing.what: Number of the 27 sweep configurations that reached 0.9 test accuracy (needed to judge the selection behind the slope of 1.01).

record.verdict_notes: The study is mostly theory. Only r1 bears on a listed version. The paper explicitly disclaims explaining the abrupt accuracy jump, dataset-size dependence, and adaptive-optimizer effects. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The benchmark tests delayed generalization on modular addition, but does not test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.
The paper does not identify or track a generalizing circuit or memorizing components, or measure circuit progress anticipating an accuracy jump.
No non-algorithmic datasets are tested, and initialization scale or weight norm is not compared as a switch between lazy and rich regimes.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
The experiments test weight-decay-dependent relaxation, but do not test whether a lower-norm efficient circuit is selected, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below it.
The study does not compare identifiable algorithms across runs.
Adaptive-optimizer and numerical-artifact explanations are not empirically tested; adaptive and preconditioned optimizers are deferred to an outlook.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular addition with full-batch heavy ball and coupled L2; report training and test accuracy over iterations.

conditions.value: heavy ball with coupled L2; β = 0.9, η = 0.2, λ = 3 × 10−4

rows.measure: Training and test accuracy over iterations
rows.value: Training accuracy reaches 1 at k ≈ 4 × 102; test accuracy passes 0.5 at k ≈ 7 × 103 and 0.9 at k ≈ 1.05 × 104; delay ratio ≈ 26; ends near 0.96–0.99.
rows.note: The reported benchmark shows training accuracy saturating well before test accuracy rises. It is one architecture and one seed.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. Chance on mod-17 is about 0.06; the final 0.96–0.99 is near-perfect. It is a single seed with one architecture, and the large-norm initialization was chosen to induce memorization-first training.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Sweep optimizer hyperparameters and measure the iteration at which test accuracy first reaches 0.9.

conditions.value: runs reaching test accuracy 0.9 within the prescribed training horizon

rows.measure: Iteration at which test accuracy first reaches 0.9 versus (1 − β)/(ηλ)
rows.note: Aggregate result across the qualifying configurations; training split is fixed, so this is not a training-set-size sweep.
rows.check: Measures how the delay scales with (1−β)/(ηλ) on a fixed training split. V1 names training-set-size dependence, not optimizer-hyperparameter dependence, so this belongs under fits_no_version. The value is also aggregated over only the runs that reached 0.9 test accuracy, a selection whose count is not stated.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Measure late test-loss-excess relaxation and compare it with the predicted null-mode rate.
rows.measure: Exponential decay rate of test-loss excess relative to its late plateau
rows.baseline: Parameter-free prediction − log ρ0 = 6.0 × 10−4 per step
rows.note: This is a loss-tail result, not a measure of circuit formation or test-accuracy delay.

rows.subject: two-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Measure the population-visible empirical-null component using projectors frozen at k = 2000.
rows.baseline: Parameter-free prediction − log ρ0 = 6.0 × 10−4 per step
rows.value: Decays several times more slowly than the prediction.
rows.note: The authors attribute the mismatch to substantial Jacobian rotation during grokking and ongoing feature learning.

rows.operation_detail: Sweep λ, η, and β; measure the grokking-component decay rate and threshold relaxation count.

rows.operation_detail: Compute training and held-out Jacobians at a post-interpolation, pre-grokking checkpoint and estimate their ranks.
rows.measure: Training Jacobian rank and population-visible part of empirical null space
rows.value: Training Jacobian is 2686 × 6528 with full row rank 2686; held-out Jacobian is 2040 × 6528; the population-visible part of the empirical null space has maximal rank at this holdout size (2040 of 2040).
rows.note: The text reports rank stability under the stated cutoffs and a stable null-space dimension; this is a kernel-geometry measurement, not circuit identification.

relationships.condition: Modular addition p = 17, width-128 quadratic MLP, squared loss, full-batch heavy ball with coupled L2, 5× init, single seed
relationships.reason: Training accuracy hits 1 at about 400 steps; test accuracy passes 0.9 only at about 10,500 steps (delay ratio ≈ 26), ending near 0.96–0.99 (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Training accuracy reached 100% around step 400, while test accuracy exceeded 90% around step 10,500, giving a timing ratio near 26 and final accuracy around 96–99%.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
